claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 shows limited amorphous retention after solidification.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 has a complex crystallization or thermal response during reheating.
Adding 2–5 at% Zr in place of part of the transition-metal content will enhance amorphous retention.
Adding 2–5 at% Zr will improve stability against crystallization during reheating.
The proposed benefit should occur at cooling rates of approximately 10^4–10^6 K/s.
Cooling sufficiently rapidly can bypass equilibrium crystallization in the proposed alloy.
At cooling rates that are too slow, crystallization will overwhelm the kinetic retardation attributed to Zr.
The Zr intervention should be effective during moderate DSC reheating rates at which crystallization kinetics are activated.
Zr addition will increase atomic-size mismatch in the alloy.
Zr addition will strengthen negative mixing enthalpy in the alloy.
The increased size mismatch and negative mixing enthalpy will disrupt short-range-order clusters that serve as crystallization nucleation sites.
Zr will increase chemical and topological disorder at the atomic level.
The increased disorder will reduce atomic mobility and rearrangement during rapid cooling and reheating.
Reduced atomic mobility and rearrangement will lower the nucleation rate of crystalline phases.
Zr may shift local short-range order toward configurations that are less conducive to crystallization.
The Zr-modified alloy will retain a larger amorphous fraction than Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 after solidification.
The Zr-modified alloy will show a delayed or higher-temperature crystallization onset during DSC reheating.
Excessive Zr addition may cause phase segregation or formation of new crystalline phases.
Short-range order is an inherent feature of multi-principal-element alloys and can persist across cooling and thermal-treatment histories.
